section_summary: This section documents U.S. State Department efforts between November 1935 and October 1938 to protect the practice rights of American attorneys residing in Japan—specifically William B. Spencer in Yokohama, William J. Sebald in Kobe, and C. C. Smith in Tokyo—under Japan's Lawyers' Law of 1933 (Law No. 53), which took effect in April 1936 and restricted legal practice to Japanese subjects except where foreign reciprocity was certified. To satisfy the Japanese Ministry of Justice, the State Department coordinated with bar and judicial authorities in the District of Columbia and Maryland to obtain authenticated certificates demonstrating that Japanese lawyers in those jurisdictions were permitted to advise their countrymen on Japanese and foreign law without formal admission to the bar. These authenticated credentials were transmitted through diplomatic instructions and urgent telegraphic instructions to Ambassador Joseph C. Grew in Tokyo for formal delivery to the Japanese Government.

subfiles.about: Diplomatic despatch transmitting and analyzing English translations of Japan's Lawyers' Law of 1933 and related legislation restricting legal practice to Japanese subjects unless reciprocity is established.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Chargé d'Affaires ad interim Edwin L. Neville reports on the newly enacted Lawyers' Law of Japan (Law No. 53 of 1933), scheduled to take effect on April 1, 1936. He notes that Articles 2 and 6 restrict the practice of law to Japanese subjects unless the Minister of Justice grants permission to foreign lawyers upon assurance of reciprocity. Neville reports having conferred with the three American lawyers currently in Japan, who practice strictly as consultants outside Japanese courts, and suggests that pending regulations might accommodate consulting work on a reciprocal basis. The despatch transmits complete English translations of Law No. 53, establishing qualifications, bar associations, rights and duties, and disciplinary courts, as well as Law No. 54 of 1933 regarding the control of handling legal affairs.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1559: Lawyers' Law of Japan (Law No. 53 of the Year 1933)

subfiles.about: A stray, isolated page fragment quoting a news report on statements by the Japanese Premier regarding Chiang Kai-shek and the territorial integrity of China.
subfiles.summary: This isolated page fragment, numbered 14, contains a single incomplete sentence and a short paragraph reporting on Chinese leader Chiang Kai-shek and Japanese foreign policy. Citing the Japanese news agency Domei, it states that the Japanese Premier affirmed that the territorial integrity of China had been advocated by Japan for forty years and that Japan must therefore prevent foreign powers from taking aggressive action against China. The fragment appears to be an unrelated document inadvertently filmed or bound into this decimal file.
subfiles.title: Fragment Regarding Japanese Policy Toward China and Chiang Kai-shek

subfiles.about: Letter from an American lawyer in Yokohama requesting State Department assistance to secure an official reciprocity certificate from the District of Columbia to satisfy the Japanese Department of Justice.
subfiles.from: William B. Spencer, Attorney-at-Law and Patent Attorney, Yokohama, Japan
subfiles.summary: William B. Spencer, an American attorney and patent attorney practicing in Yokohama, writes to the Secretary of State on behalf of himself, C. C. Smith of Tokyo, and William J. Sebald of Kobe regarding their applications for permits under Article 6 of Japan's Lawyers' Law of 1933. Spencer explains that although he submitted a letter dated February 19, 1936 from John Paul Earnest, Chairman of the Committee on Admissions and Grievances of the District of Columbia Bar, the Japanese Department of Justice required certification by a recognized U.S. government department or ambassador, similar to a certificate obtained by British barrister John Gadsby. Emphasizing that American attorneys represent major U.S. commercial interests in Japan—such as Universal Pictures, Carnation, IBM, and Dollar Steamship Line—Spencer asks the State Department to certify that Japanese lawyers may advise their countrymen in the District of Columbia without appearing in court. The letter is accompanied by copies of the Earnest letter and the British certificate, along with duplicate carbon copies.
subfiles.title: Letter from William B. Spencer Regarding Permission to Practice Law in Japan Under the Lawyers' Law of 1933
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, Washington (Attention: Mr. Ward, Legal Department)

subfiles.about: Short letter from William B. Spencer providing his temporary lodging address in Washington, D.C. while pursuing his petition.
subfiles.summary: William B. Spencer advises Mr. Ward in the State Department that while his formal letter to the Secretary of State was typed on his Yokohama office stationery, he is currently staying in Washington, D.C. to follow up on his request. He gives his temporary address as care of Mr. William C. Smith at 5100 Fifth Street, N.W., Washington, D.C.
subfiles.title: Letter from William B. Spencer Providing Temporary Address in Washington, D.C.

subfiles.about: State Department letter informing William B. Spencer that an authenticated chain of certificates establishing reciprocity in the District of Columbia has been forwarded to Tokyo.
subfiles.from: Green H. Hackworth, Legal Adviser (For the Secretary of State)
subfiles.summary: Legal Adviser Green H. Hackworth replies to William B. Spencer's letter of June 27, 1938 and his personal call at the Department of State regarding the reciprocity certificate required under Japanese Law No. 53 of 1933. Hackworth explains that since the right to practice law in the District of Columbia is governed by the Committee on Admissions and Grievances rather than the Department of State or Justice, an official chain of certification was prepared: a statement dated June 27, 1938 by Committee Chairman John Paul Earnest, certified by the Chief Justice of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, authenticated by the Attorney General under the seal of the Department of Justice, and authenticated under the seal of the Department of State. Spencer is informed that these documents have been forwarded to the American Ambassador at Tokyo with instructions to request the Japanese Department of Justice to issue Spencer's practice permit.
subfiles.title: Letter from Legal Adviser Green H. Hackworth to William B. Spencer

subfiles.about: Diplomatic instruction transmitting authenticated District of Columbia credentials to Ambassador Joseph C. Grew in Tokyo to secure William B. Spencer's law practice permit.
subfiles.from: R. Walton Moore (For the Secretary of State)
subfiles.summary: The Department of State instructs Ambassador Joseph C. Grew to intervene on behalf of William B. Spencer, an American attorney who has practiced in Japan for seventeen years, in his application under Article 6 of Japan's Lawyers' Law of 1933. The instruction reviews the Japanese Department of Justice's demand for official government certification of the authority of John Paul Earnest, Chairman of the District of Columbia Committee on Admissions and Grievances. Transmitting Spencer's petition, Earnest's statement of June 27, 1938, and authentications from the Chief Justice of the District Court, the Attorney General, and the Secretary of State, the Department directs the Ambassador to deliver the documents to the Japanese Ministry of Justice through appropriate channels and request issuance of the permit.
subfiles.title: Instruction No. 1530 to Ambassador Joseph C. Grew Regarding William B. Spencer's Practice of Law in Japan
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo

subfiles.about: Letter from a Baltimore attorney submitting Maryland bar reciprocity certificates on behalf of William J. Sebald and requesting an urgent cable to Tokyo.
subfiles.from: George V. Parkhurst, Attorney at Law, Baltimore, Maryland
keywords: Maryland State Board of Law Examiners
subfiles.summary: Baltimore attorney George V. Parkhurst submits legal documents to the Department of State on behalf of William J. Sebald of the Kobe firm DeBecker, DeBecker & Sebald, seeking to establish reciprocity between Maryland and Japan under Japanese Law No. 53 of 1933. Parkhurst delivers an October 3, 1938 letter from Alexander Armstrong, Chairman of the Maryland State Board of Law Examiners, along with supporting certificates from Chief Judge Carroll T. Bond and Clerk James A. Young of the Maryland Court of Appeals, authenticated by the Secretary of State of Maryland. Because Sebald was given a two-month deadline expiring around November 5, 1938 to produce proof of reciprocity, Parkhurst urges the Department to immediately cable the Embassy in Tokyo to notify the Japanese Minister of Justice that the Maryland papers are en route. Attached are Armstrong's letter stating that Japanese lawyers may advise their countrymen in Maryland and Judge Bond's certificate of October 11, 1938 verifying Armstrong's authority.
subfiles.title: Letter from George V. Parkhurst Transmitting Maryland Reciprocity Documents for William J. Sebald

subfiles.about: Telegraphic instruction to the Embassy in Tokyo directing it to inform the Japanese Minister of Justice and William J. Sebald that Maryland reciprocity documents are in transit.
subfiles.summary: The Department of State instructs the American Embassy in Tokyo by confidential cable to notify both the Japanese Minister of Justice and American attorney William J. Sebald in Kobe that authenticated certificates of competent Maryland officials are being mailed. The telegram explains that the documents establish that Japanese lawyers in Maryland are accorded rights substantially identical to those recognized in the District of Columbia in the earlier Spencer case.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 353 to American Embassy, Tokyo, Regarding William J. Sebald

subfiles.about: State Department letter to George V. Parkhurst confirming the authentication of the Maryland certificates and the dispatch of an urgent cable to Tokyo on Sebald's behalf.
subfiles.from: Department of State (For the Secretary of State)
subfiles.summary: The Department of State acknowledges George V. Parkhurst's letter of October 12, 1938 and the accompanying Maryland certificates regarding the rights accorded Japanese lawyers in Maryland. The Department confirms that certificates under the seal of the Department of State authenticating the Maryland state seal have been attached and forwarded to the American Embassy in Tokyo for presentation to the Japanese Ministry of Justice. In view of the tight deadline set by the Japanese authorities, the letter includes a paraphrase of the telegram sent to the Tokyo Embassy on October 14, 1938 notifying the Minister of Justice and Sebald that the authenticated documents are on the way.
subfiles.title: Letter from Department of State to George V. Parkhurst Regarding William J. Sebald

subfiles.about: Diplomatic instruction transmitting authenticated Maryland bar certificates to Ambassador Joseph C. Grew in Tokyo to support William J. Sebald's application to practice law.
subfiles.from: R. Walton Moore (For the Secretary of State)
subfiles.summary: Confirming its telegram No. 353 of October 14, 1938, the Department of State transmits to Ambassador Joseph C. Grew a copy of George V. Parkhurst's letter and seven authenticated documents demonstrating that Japanese lawyers in Maryland enjoy rights substantially identical to those available in the District of Columbia. The enclosed documents include the letter of Alexander Armstrong, certificates by Chief Judge Carroll T. Bond and Clerk James A. Young, authentications by Maryland Secretary of State E. Ray Jones, and authentications of the Maryland seal under the seal of the Department of State. Ambassador Grew is requested to submit these documents through official channels to the Japanese Ministry of Justice and request the issuance of the practice permit applied for by William J. Sebald.
subfiles.title: Instruction No. 1598 to Ambassador Joseph C. Grew Regarding William J. Sebald's Application
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo

subfiles.about: Letter expressing thanks to Legal Adviser Green H. Hackworth for the State Department's swift cooperation in William J. Sebald's reciprocity matter.
subfiles.from: George V. Parkhurst, Attorney at Law, Baltimore, Maryland
subfiles.summary: George V. Parkhurst acknowledges receipt of the Department of State's communication of October 17, 1938 regarding William J. Sebald. He expresses sincere appreciation on behalf of Sebald and himself for the Department's prompt, invaluable assistance and cooperative handling of the matter.
subfiles.title: Letter from George V. Parkhurst to Secretary of State (Attention: Green H. Hackworth)
subfiles.to: The Secretary of State (Attention: Mr. Green H. Hackworth)

subfiles.about: Letter thanking State Department desk officer Mr. Ward for his assistance in transmitting cables and documents to Japan on behalf of William J. Sebald.
subfiles.from: George V. Parkhurst, Attorney at Law, Baltimore, Maryland
subfiles.summary: George V. Parkhurst acknowledges receipt of the October 17th communication from Legal Adviser Green H. Hackworth confirming the issuance of a cable to Tokyo. Parkhurst extends personal thanks to Mr. Ward in the Department's legal section for his helpful cooperation and vital assistance in facilitating the communication to the Japanese Minister of Justice.
subfiles.title: Letter from George V. Parkhurst to Department of State (Attention: Mr. Ward)
